correctness.rationale: For a hub-free coalition R, exact payoff 2e_H(R)/|R| ≤ |R|/2 with equality precisely for an edge, using degree≤2 and exclusion of 3- and 4-cycles. For hub coalition {h}∪S, 2(|S|+e_H(S))/(|S|+1) ≤ 1+|S|/2 with equality only for |S|=2 with one edge or |S|=3 with a P3. Summing gives bound, and equality reduces bijectively to a perfect matching after deleting the motif. Explicit unilateral deviation cases verify every equality partition Nash stable; rational finite programs independently check representative and all nonisomorphic eligible graphs up to seven base vertices. Short-cycle exceptions are explicitly excluded or handled separately.

evidence: Hanaka–Ikeyama–Ono provide algorithms for tree-like and bounded-treewidth inputs, and thus computational coverage but not the asserted explicit optimizer structure.
Bilò et al. prove optimal-partition stability on trees, but the present G contains triangles and is not a tree.
Bazgan et al. treat degree-two whole graphs and high-minimum-degree graphs; arbitrary K_1∨H of this theorem need be neither.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Algorithmic solvability is logically weaker than an exact formula, description and count of all equality partitions plus stability. Tree Nash-stability does not apply to graphs containing hub-created triangles. Dense-graph min-degree conditions fail for long fans and wheels.

originality.rationale: Original contribution is the exact hub-motif/matching equivalence, a bijective optimizer count, and Nash stability of every sharp optimum for the apex of any maximum-degree-two graph without 3- or 4-cycles. These are not consequences of the algorithmic bounded-treewidth treatment in Hanaka–Ikeyama–Ono, nor the tree-only stability theorem of Bilò et al.; degree-two or high-minimum-degree input results in Bazgan–Casel–Cazals do not imply this apex-graph structural characterization. Search coverage and residual literature risks are explicit, and database absence is not a priority proof.

value.rationale: The theorem explains exactly when a universal-vertex social-network game retains the optimal matching-based welfare threshold, classifies every extremizing coalition structure, counts them by a graph-matching certificate, and proves optimal Nash stability. Sharp wheel and fan counts and failed-certificate boundary are natural interpretable outputs, not arbitrary small-parameter statistics.
